segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri and the peace chants began with a map: two verbs, dhimahi, we hold in mind, and prachodayat, may he stir. Today, the very first word.

A text arrives with no photo and no link, just two words: that one. So you scroll up, hunting for whatever that is. The Gayatri opens the same way. Its first word is tat, that. And here's the odd part: the thing it points at doesn't show up next. Or after that. Two more words go by, the line ends, and only at the start of the next line does the noun arrive. A verse that begins by pointing at something it hasn't named yet. Why build it that way?
screen: `A TEXT THAT JUST SAYS: THAT ONE.`
`TAT: THAT.` → `THE NOUN IS A LINE AWAY.`

segments.voice: Start with how a reader solves it. Tat is a pointing word, that, aimed away from the speaker, over there. So, that what? The verse makes you wait: savitur, of Savitr; varenyam, worth choosing. Then, first word of the second line: bhargo, radiance. That's the noun tat belongs to. How does a reader know? Agreement. Bhargas, radiance, is a neuter word, neither he nor she, and tat is the neuter form of that. Varenyam wears the same neuter ending. The three match, like teammates in the same jersey scattered across a field. So the reader holds tat open, carries it past two words, and closes it at bhargo. Now the puzzle's answer, as far as the text goes. The verse names a direction before it names a thing. It says that, not this: the radiance isn't already in hand. It's over there, and the line leans toward it. The waiting is part of the reading. This path has met the same small word before, in the Chandogya Upanishad: tat tvam asi, that, you are. Same pointing word, a different sentence around it. Here, in the Gayatri, tat only points, and the whole first line turns the way it points.
screen: `TAT POINTS AWAY: THAT, OVER THERE.` · `SAME NEUTER ENDING, SAME TEAM.` · `HOLD IT OPEN UNTIL BHARGO.` · `A DIRECTION BEFORE A THING.` · then, large: `THE VERSE POINTS BEFORE IT NAMES.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on the farthest thing you can see: a window, a doorway, the far wall. Silently call it only that, without naming it. Keep your gaze there, soft and steady, facing toward it while the time runs.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: tat, that, the pointing word that waits a whole line for its noun.

notes: Gayatri word by word: tat. Grammar stated: tat as neuter nominative/accusative singular of the demonstrative, agreeing with neuter bhargas (bhargo by sandhi) and vareṇyam. Confirm wording for learners.
'The first word' means of RV 3.62.10 itself, not counting Om bhur bhuvah svah, which day 1265 explained sits outside the verse.
The Chandogya link is only that the same word appears; the script makes no claim that teachers read the Gayatri's tat through tat tvam asi.
